summary: Defines MIB objects, in SMIv2 format, for managing relational database management system implementations with SNMP. This standards-track document lets network management tools monitor database servers in a common way.

plainLanguage.summary: A set of standard gauges so one tool can check how different database programs are doing.

questions: how to monitor a database with snmp
what traps does the rdbms mib define
subtitle: A standard SNMP vocabulary for asking any relational database about its size, servers, settings, limits and state.

tldr.problem: Each database product exposes its own management data, so a network management tool cannot monitor database servers from different vendors in a common way.
tldr.mechanism: The RDBMS-MIB defines nine tables, written in SMIv2, that describe installed and open databases, servers, configuration parameters, limited resources and the links between servers and databases, plus two traps.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from August 1994. It covers generic monitoring only and expects vendor-specific MIBs for detailed management.

today: RFC 1697 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1994, and the record lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is built on the SNMPv2 framework documents such as RFC 1442 and RFC 1565.

sections.title: What the RDBMS-MIB Is
sections.content:
RFC 1697 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols. It describes managed objects for relational database management system (RDBMS) implementations. The module is named rdbmsMIB and sits at { mib-2 39 }.

It holds information on installed databases, servers, and the relation between the two. The RFC says the entities are broadly applicable and enough for many monitoring tasks, but far from adequate for detailed management or performance monitoring of a specific product. That gap is expected to be filled by vendor and product specific MIBs.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a shared list of questions you can ask any database, like what is your name, how big are you and are you running.

sections.title: The SNMPv2 Framework Underneath
sections.content:
The module is written for the SNMPv2 Network Management Framework, which the RFC breaks into four components. RFC 1442 defines the SMI, the way objects are described and named. RFC 1213 (STD 17) defines MIB-II, the core set of managed objects. RFC 1445 covers administrative and architectural aspects, RFC 1448 defines the protocol used to reach managed objects, and RFC 1443 describes textual conventions.

Objects live in a virtual information store, the MIB, and are defined with a subset of ASN.1. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, and the type together with an instance identifies one specific instantiation. The RDBMS-MIB is also presented as an extension of RFC 1565, the MIB for monitoring network service applications.
sections.plainLanguage: There is already a rulebook for how to describe things that can be measured. This MIB follows it, so any tool that knows the rulebook can read it.

sections.title: Vendors, Databases, Servers and Associations
sections.content:
The RFC defines its terms before using them. A database, for this MIB, is a collection of tables whose organisation is based on the relational model. A server is an entity that provides access to databases and can exist independently of other servers; it may or may not be a single process. Servers are tied to the APPLICATION-MIB of RFC 1565 and indexed by its applIndex.

Vendors and products supply database systems on a host, and a host may have several vendors or several systems from one vendor. Each may have a private MIB, which can be located with the PrivateMibOID objects. Inbound associations are local or remote conversations, usually SQL CONNECT statements, but the MIB does not reveal individual associations. It only offers association counters.

Servers and databases can relate in every obvious way: one database to one server, one database to many servers, many databases to one server, or many to many.
sections.plainLanguage: A database is a filing cabinet, a server is the clerk who opens it, and the MIB keeps a list of which clerks can open which cabinets.

sections.title: The Nine Tables
sections.content:
The module is organised into nine tables, twelve potentially writable objects and two traps. Four tables concern databases, four concern servers, and one relates them:

  • rdbmsDbTable: databases installed on a host
  • rdbmsDbInfoTable: actively opened databases
  • rdbmsDbParamTable: database configuration parameters
  • rdbmsDbLimitedResourceTable: database limited resources
  • rdbmsSrvTable: database servers installed on a system
  • rdbmsSrvInfoTable: active database servers
  • rdbmsSrvParamTable: server configuration parameters
  • rdbmsSrvLimitedResourceTable: server limited resources
  • rdbmsRelTable: relation of servers and databases on a host

The database info table reports a product name, a version, size units (bytes, kbytes, mbytes, gbytes or tbytes, all binary multiples where 1K = 1024), allocated and used size, and the time of the last backup. The server info table holds counters such as disk reads and writes, logical reads and writes, page reads and writes, handled requests, finished transactions and out-of-space events, and also the start-up time and inbound association figures.
sections.plainLanguage: There are nine lists. Some describe the databases, some describe the servers, and one says which server can open which database.

sections.title: Parameters and Limited Resources
sections.content:
The parameter tables hold configuration settings, each identified by a product-specific name of 1 to 64 characters, a subindex, an optional ID that may be described in another MIB, the current value and a comment. A parameter with a variable number of members, such as members of the DBA user group, must be shown as a set of rows. A set of choices that always fits in the 255 character length of a DisplayString may be a comma separated list with subindex one. Zero may not be a subindex.

The limited resource tables cover resources with a maximum set by a parameter, such as the number of available locks or disk space on a partition. Each row reports the limit, the current level, a high water mark, a failure counter and a description. Resources shared across databases belong in the server table. The RFC also defines one well-known resource, rdbmsLogSpace, for storage allocated for redo and undo logs.
sections.plainLanguage: Settings are like the dials on a machine, and limited resources are like a fuel tank that shows how much is left and how often it ran dry.

sections.title: Server-Database State and Traps
sections.content:
The relation table is indexed by database index and then applIndex, so walking it with get-next or get-bulk finds all servers able to serve a given database. Each row has an rdbmsRelState with five values: other(1), active(2), available(3), restricted(4) and unavailable(5), plus the time the server made the database active. A database counts as actively opened when at least one of its relation states is active.

Two traps are defined. rdbmsStateChange signals that a server/database pair moved to a less accessible state, where both active and available count as fully accessible, and it carries the new state. rdbmsOutOfSpace signals that a server could not allocate space for a database, and the RFC warns to take care not to flood the network with these traps.

Objects for inactive or missing items may answer with noSuchName (SNMPv1) or noSuchInstance (SNMPv2).
sections.plainLanguage: Each pairing of server and database has a status like running, ready, limited or off. When a status gets worse, the system can send a quick alert.

sections.title: Writable Objects and Compliance
sections.content:
The MIB requires no writable objects for conformance, and there is no expectation that an RDBMS is actively managed through it. An implementer may allow writes to twelve objects, including contacts, allocated database size, parameter values and comments, resource limits and descriptions, and the maximum inbound associations of a server.

The compliance statement requires the rdbmsGroup, with write access optional for each of those objects (minimum access is read-only). Compliant systems also need the hrSystem group of the HOST-RESOURCES-MIB and the applGroup of the APPLICATION-MIB. The two traps are intentionally left out of every conformance group.
sections.plainLanguage: Looking at the gauges is required. Turning the knobs is optional, and an agent may refuse.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. Because some objects can be writable, how access is controlled is left to the management framework and the implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not say how to keep strangers from reading or changing the gauges.

items.label: other
items.desc: Some other condition, possibly described in the vendor private MIB.

items.label: active
items.desc: The server is actively using the database.

items.label: available
items.desc: The server could use the database if necessary.

items.label: restricted
items.desc: The database is in an administratively determined state of less-than-complete availability.

items.label: unavailable
items.desc: The database is not available through this server.
